items.title: Nodusfall looks like Elden Ring but was "designed to be accessible," says HoYoverse: "We don't want difficulty to be a barrier"
items.content:
The Genshin Impact devs aren't looking to put people through the wringer

(Image credit: HoYoverse) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The makers of Genshin Impact and Zenless Zone Zero are taking a different route for upcoming action game Nodusfall, going for a more of a downtrodden, Elden Ring vibe. Although it seems grim and scary, HoYoverse states the adventure isn't meant to be impenetrably hard.

The studio takes to Twitter to answer a few frequently asked questions of the upcoming release. "We don't want difficulty to be a barrier for players entering Nodusfall," the post reads.

"The game is designed to be accessible even for players who are new to this type of action gameplay," it continues, "while still maintaining a high ceiling in terms of controls, coordination, and builds, giving players who love a challenge plenty of room to dive deeper."

It's been nearly a month since the first reveal, and we've collected ten questions from the comments that everyone wants to know about. Let's talk about them.Q: What kind of game is Nodusfall?A: Simply put, it's a mythology-themed action game centered around multiplayer co-op.… September 23, 2026

The line about people who're unfamiliar with the trappings of challenging action games is important here, because there are inevitably going to be converts. Zenless Zone Zero, Genshin Impact, and Honkai: Star Rail each have massive communities, a portion of which will very likely hop into Nodusfall to check it out.

Going for the complete FromSoftware experience and putting everyone through an absolute gauntlet in the first hour probably won't do much for player retention. We don't need everyone to sit through HoYoverse's version of the Undead Burg, inching forward bit by bit.

Genshin Impact devs' new action game Nodusfall feels like Elden Ring Nightreign at home, but don't write it off yet Nodusfall looks more like Monster Hunter and Elden Ring than games from Genshin Impact's Hoyoverse Nodusfall isn't a gacha game, Mihoyo confirms The use of the term "accessible" suggests there'll be a number of settings people can tinker with to make the experience comfortable to themselves. Such options are always welcome, and that's coming from someone who loves a good gauntlet.

Further details on Nodusfall are limited, but we know it's a co-op focused game that sits somewhere between FromSoft's output and Monster Hunter, since the overall goal is to take down gigantic beasts roaming the land. Done well, it could be very captivating – though I suspect many of us will be dying plenty of times regardless.

items.title: Review: Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition (Switch 2)
items.summary: Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition on Nintendo Switch 2 brings a masterful action-RPG to new shores - a surprisingly polished package despite some minor technical drawbacks, but nonetheless a worthwhile journey, especially for newcomers.
items.content:
You are using an outdated browser. Please upgrade your browser to improve your experience.

What can I say about Elden Ring that hasn’t already been said? From Software’s magnum opus originally released in 2022 to massive critical acclaim, redefining open-world action-RPGs forever. After a gargantuan expansion with Shadow of the Erdtree and a successful co-op multiplayer endeavour with Nightreign , From Software now extends Elden Ring ’s reach over to the Nintendo Switch 2 to mostly great results. Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition combines both the base game and the expansion, Shadow of the Erdtree , along with all previously released updates and new content, in one excellent package. If you want to read more about what makes Elden Ring so exceptional, I have an entire standalone review (as well as for Shadow of the Erdtree ) you can check out, because this review is more focused on the technical aspects of Elden Ring running on Nintendo Switch 2. Performance-wise, Elden Ring on Switch 2 initially drew some scepticism. Early impressions of outlets getting hands-on time with the game running in handheld weren’t very optimistic. Many reported bugs and frequent framerate dips that sometimes got as low as 20fps. For the longest time, it seemed like Nintendo’s next-gen hardware was ill-equipped to handle the game. I’m happy to report that From Software used all of its spare time to fine-tune the game on Switch 2 because the end-product is honestly commendable, but not without faults. Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition combines both the base game and the expansion, Shadow of the Erdtree , along with all previously released updates and new content, in one excellent package. There had to be some caveats to get Elden Ring running on Switch 2 and unfortunately, that came with a downsizing of the target framerate. Unlike its PC/console counterpart, Elden Ring ’s Switch 2 version ultimately targets 30fps instead of 60fps though results may vary. In my experience, there were instances where the framerate did exceed 30fps but it never hit the smoother 60fps I wanted. This is most noticeable playing the game docked and during open world stretches of exploration, as the framerate sometimes struggled to stay consistent but it hovers around the 30-35fps mark without many significant dips below that point. The real kicker is whether 30fps is enough to be effective in boss fights. Elden Ring has no shortage of these spectacular boss encounters that often require pin-point precision and movement from players. Thankfully, 30fps doesn’t seem to hurt the experience at all. Like playing Bloodborne , your brain eventually recalibrates itself to flow with the lower framerate and it shouldn’t be long before you’re as effective and skilled as you were on other platforms. For newcomers, this will barely be an issue. In handheld mode, the Switch 2’s VRR somewhat alleviates the framerate fluctuations and it might be the preferred way to play the game for many. On a smaller screen, the image quality and visual fidelity is noticeably more vibrant and colourful, with less instances of texture pop-ins or framerate stutters, though they’re still present. When you get to in-door sections or dungeons, thankfully things smoothen out and there’s barely any technical hiccups worth stressing over. The most immediate differences are going to be the visuals and overall texture quality. Perhaps it’s unfair to directly compare it to its console counterparts since I could only boot up my Xbox Series X and PS5 Pro to see side-by-side comparisons - two powerful consoles offering a notably more consistent and stable version of the game - but the downgrades on Switch 2 are only noticeable if you really look for them. Otherwise, despite the framerate dips, this is a remarkable port that surprised me in unexpected ways. In handheld mode, the Switch 2’s VRR somewhat alleviates the framerate fluctuations and it might be the preferred way to play the game for many. Apart from the novelty of playing Elden Ring on the go, the Switch 2 version also offers some neat new content. Two new starting classes, the Heavy Knight and the Idus Knight, give you a bit more flexibility starting out with a build. I opted to choose the Heavy Knight and build a tanky, greatsword-swinging Tarnished, but you can really choose any direction to go when it comes to build-crafting in the game - one of its most appealing selling points. On top of the new classes, you can also now customise your spectral steed with cool mounts but these are merely cosmetic cherries on top of an already delicious cake. Additionally, new in-game events spot the Lands Between like new NPC invasion points - and trust me, they’re a brutal challenge if you actively go out looking for them. The biggest draw of Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition is the fact that this is, by all accounts, the most “definitive” edition of the game out today. The base game, expansion, and new DLC all contribute to a staggering action-RPG absolutely worthy of its asking price, easily providing hundreds of hours of gameplay if you’re looking to explore and try out everything. For newcomers to the Soulslike genre, as tough as Elden Ring gets (and it gets unreasonably tough at times), I can’t think of a better jumping-in point for the genre since its open world structure and very lenient build flexibility means you’ll always have options on how to progress. Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition on Nintendo Switch 2 brings a masterful action-RPG to new shores, stacked with new and old content. It’s a surprisingly polished package, despite some of the technical drawbacks needed to get the game working well on the Switch 2. Most of all, it’s just a solid deal for Switch 2 players looking to experience one of the best games ever made and have the novelty of carrying it around wherever you go. items.title: Elden Ring Nightreign is dead, but modders are dabbing on its corpse, with one porting an entire Dark Souls 2 DLC zone as a playable map
items.summary: A new spin on an old favorite.
items.content:

(Image credit: FromSoftware) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 33 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Modder Doneda has released a particularly funky and exciting mod for Elden Ring Nightreign, porting Dark Souls 2's Frozen Eleum Loyce and Frigid Outskirts as a standalone map. They also have a trailer up for the project on YouTube. Doneda's a bit of a Dark Souls 2 expert⁠—they previously restored the remains of a cut sewers map to the sequel for demonstration purposes.

Watch On Gun to my head, I think the Brume Tower is my favorite DS2 level, but Eleum Loyce still feels like a dear old friend. I enjoyed base DS2 more than most, but the Lost Crowns DLCs were on a whole different level. Other FromSoft DLCs may be better in a vacuum (Old Hunters, Shadow of the Erdtree), but there has never been a more staggering, exhilarating leap in quality between one of the studio's games and its corresponding expansion.

While Brume Tower may be my beautiful baby, it just wouldn't fit in Nightreign like Eleum Loyce does: The wide open Outskirts and walled city can mimic the mini open world of Limveld in a way the twisty, narrow Brume Tower couldn't manage. My favorite detail is that it looks like the night two circle narrows down on the underground chaos arena where you fight the Burnt Ivory King , a fun and creative recontextualizing of the level's original flow.

Doneda's new map is already available for download on the Nightreign Nexus. You'll need to install Mod Engine 3 beforehand to run it⁠—most, if not all Nightreign mods require the utility. Doneda seems intent on making more modded Nightreign maps, and you can follow their work on YouTube or support them via Ko-fi .

You talk about love/hate relationships, I'd say I have a ⅔ hate, ⅓ love relationship with Nightreign. Its Deep of Night update gave me and my friends incentive to keep playing, while it introduces some truly incredible boss fights⁠—stuff like The Balancers and Libra give me hope that FromSoft can still surprise, delight, and challenge in a post-Promised Consort world.

Elden Ring's Tarnished Edition is exciting enough on its own, but it's also our last chance to properly experience the game's launch day hype Elden Ring players are hard at work putting the new Tarnished Edition DLC's gear to the test I'm a decade-plus FromSoftware sicko, and these are my 5 takeaways from the first Duskbloods gameplay But Deep of Night also subjected us to the most frustrating, artless version of FromSoftware difficulty I've yet seen, and the studio appears to have quietly stopped supporting the game to work on The Duskbloods⁠—and hopefully something else, too?

Perhaps I should take the glass half full view of FromSoft releasing a multiplayer game, supporting it a bit, but not feeling compelled to turn it into a forever empire of live service returns. In the absence of official support, though, there have been some weird, exciting things happening with Nightreign. Yui's Nightreign iteration of her signature Seamless Co-op mod is a welcome addition for more "chill with your friends" -style play, while I've been intrigued by gameplay videos of TerraMag's SotE and ds3 weapons , a "no duh" addition that I'm still surprised FromSoft didn't manage itself.

items.title: HoYoverse's Nodusfall might look like Elden Ring, but there's a promising dark fantasy action game here that took me by surprise
items.summary: Nodusfall, aesthetically at least, is about as far from a typical HoYoverse game as you can get. Gone are the bright co…
items.content:
Image credit: miHoYo/HoYoverse Preview by Lottie Lynn Guides Editor Published on Sept. 19, 2026, 9 a.m. 7 comments Follow Nodus Fall Prioritise us on Google Nodusfall, aesthetically at least, is about as far from a typical HoYoverse game as you can get. Gone are the bright colours, cute creatures, and bountiful anime women. In their place, we get all the familiar trappings of dark fantasy: mysterious magics, vicious monsters, and a dingier kind of realism that - and I'm sure we've all thought it - feels a little bit Elden Ring . But from what I played at Gamescom, Nodusfall has the potential to shake off those FromSoftware comparisons and come into its own.

I'll admit to being a little worried at the beginning of my preview after learning it would consist of two boss battles fought in groups of four. After all, the majority of my co-op experience comes from RuneScape , a 25-year-old MMORPG primarily played with a mouse, and nobody wants to let their team down.

But first came the character selection. There were four options available in my demo: two focused around melee combat, two ranged. Both combat styles offered one character with healing-focused abilities which I immediately discounted - too much responsibility. The archer with a mechanical arm though? Inflicting heavy damage from a distance while taking care of any nasty surprises was definitely something I could do. Decision made, it was time to discover how my chosen role would actually play out in battle.

Nodusfall's combat, it turns out, is easy enough to get to grips with. There's your basic attack, which fills a gauge that eventually allows you to unleash a more powerful attack. Next, a secondary move. For my archer, this was a nifty - and enjoyable - bomb arrow which, once embedded in a foe's flesh, dealt extra when hit. Beyond that, each character has four unique abilities that operate based on cooldowns, some more generous than others.

My archer, for example, had an ability that essentially acted as a dodge - enabling her to jump backwards before firing off a powerful arrow - and another where she unleashed a spirit wolf. Since the wolf only deals damage in close quarters, I'd first have to dash towards a foe before using it, then follow it up with the dodge to regain some distance. All this, I should add, depletes stamina, but the bar is a generous one.

And I was thrilled to discover my archer had actual range. I could easily run around the edges of the battlefield, safe in the knowledge my attacks would still land - useful for self-preservation and for helping my fellow teammates out. If a teammate was in need of additional firepower or revival, I could easily weave myself back into the midst of battle. And in this way, it wasn't long before I found myself settling into Nodusfall's surprisingly satisfying fighting rhythm.

As for what you'll be fighting, Nodusfall's enemy design draws inspiration from different mythologies around the world. In the demo, for instance, I fought Qiongqi, a creature from Chinese mythology depicted here as a griffin-like beast, and the Maldrake, your more traditional dragon. And HoYoverse has crafted some truly impressive monster encounters that I found myself wanting to stop and properly appreciate - which is pretty hard when the object of your appreciation is also trying to bite your head off.

Each boss battle is structured the way you'd typically expect - multiple stages, each with a new health bar - but, out of the two, the Maldrake was by far my favourite. Since it's a dragon, it attacks by doing the typical dragon things: fire-breathing, jaw-snapping, wing-whacking. Yet, during the fight's opening stage, I noticed something a little bit odd: human-like arms protruding from its chest. The secret behind these arms reveals itself about midway through the battle, when a knight rips itself out of the Maldrake's torso, killing it in the process. Thus the Maldrake fight becomes the Maldrake Knight fight.

Compared to the fairly slow and predictable dragon, the Maldrake Knight is a dangerously fast sword and polearm wielder who you don't want to get cornered by. It can also unleash puddles of black goo, which sap your health if stepped in. All of the strategies I'd been developing for the dragon had to be immediately thrown aside in order to adapt to this very different enemy who just loved tossing people in the air. And I hope HoYoverse can bring the same fun unpredictability to other fights, creating a similar need for experimentation.

Of course, given Nodusfall is a free-to-play title from a studio best known for its gacha games, there are questions to be asked about how this will be monetised. The developer says characters will be unlockable via continuous play rather than the banner system other HoYoverse games like Genshin Impact employ, and so cosmetic monetisation is being considered. Beyond that, however, specifics are limited so we'll have to wait to learn more.

I didn't know what to expect going into Nodusfall's preview, but I had a surprisingly great time. Combat is fast-paced without ever becoming overwhelming, bosses are compelling, and co-op is engaging while remaining approachable. I am, though, curious to learn more about solo play. As to whether Nodusfall can carve out its own niche among the games it's clearly drawing inspiration from, that remains to be seen. From what I've played, though, it's looking promising and I'll be watching its progress during the coming year.

This preview is based on a preview at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany. HoYoverse provided flights and accommodation.

items.title: Soulslike Games: The Finest FromSoftware RPGs and Games Like Dark Souls
items.summary: From Bloodborne and Elden Ring to Mortal Shell 2 and Lies of P, here are our favourite soulslike games.
items.content:
Welcome, Dear Reader, to my guide to soulslike games. Given how close these marvellous games are to roguelikes, I figured it was time to highlight the best that I’ve played – and if you include Mike and Ric, it’s quite a few between us!

With soulslike games and roguelites often overlapping heavily in terms of structure, challenge, and progression, a round-up of our personal favourites felt like the most natural continuation of our coverage here on Rogueliker.

For this article, I’ll be focusing on the cream of the crop, covering standout releases by FromSoftware and beyond, and there’s some indie standouts waiting at the end of the feature for good measure.

As with all of the top lists here at Rogueliker, I’ve played all of the games that I have included, and I won’t write about titles that I’ve not tried just to make up the numbers. My longtime collaborators Mike Holmes and Ricardo Estevez have contributed a few entries, too, but we’ve made sure to make it clear which ones are theirs.

But first, so we’re all on the same page, I should define what I mean by the word “soulslike”, which has come to define a whole sub-genre of gaming.

The term is derived from Dark Souls, and it refers to a game that has the same gameplay characteristics as FromSoftware’s classic RPG. That game was released back in 2011, and it stands as a milestone in the genre. Not only that, but it spawned a flurry of similarly punishing action games. Here are some common features that nearly all of the titles in this article share, and that make them soulslike games:

With that out of the way, let’s move on to our very first pick…

Marking the biggest evolution of the series since its inception, Elden Ring took the industry by storm when it launched in 2022, earning GOTY awards from across the industry.

Moving from more structured, linear levels to a vast open world gave players the freedom to forge their own paths, removing the frustration of being stuck on a single boss. Mounted on your trusty steed, Torrent, you can easily lose hours roaming the Lands Between, taking on mini-bosses, searching for upgrades, and delving deeper into its rich lore – another area where Elden Ring excels when compared to its fellow soulslike games.

Speaking of lore, Elden Ring was crafted in collaboration with legendary author and Game of Thrones creator, George R.R. Martin, making for one of the most badass partnerships in gaming history.

The fact that Bloodborne remains a PS4 exclusive 11 years after its launch is, in my eyes, absolutely criminal. This gothic horror masterpiece has long stood as one of the best soulslike games for me, holding a special place as my introduction to the genre.

Combat is brutal and fast-paced, encouraging aggressive strikes over shield-blocking, unlike earlier Dark Souls titles. Its risk-reward regain system makes for truly nail-biting encounters as you can land attacks quickly to recover lost health, but misstep and you’ll be torn apart.

Praise also needs to be given to the hauntingly immersive world of Yharnam. In the grip of a deadly plague, this shadowy Victorian-era metropolis is packed with some of the most memorable locations and nightmarish bosses the series has ever seen, making exploration just as thrilling as combat itself.

Roguelike fans will also get a kick out of the game’s Chalice Dungeons. These randomly generated dungeons feature exclusive bosses you won’t find in the main story and provide an excellent way to farm Blood Echoes, materials, and other valuable rewards.

items.title: New Elden Ring Mini Replicas Arrive: Malenia, Messmer & Wylder

Tarnished, collectors, and champions of the Lands Between, we're excited to unveil a new lineup of premium 1/3 Scale Mini Replicas inspired by some of the most iconic designs from the Elden Ring universe and crafted by Pure Arts. From the legendary Blade of Miquella, to the fearsome Messmer the Impaler, and the indominable warriors of Nightreign, these finely crafted collectibles capture the artistry and atmosphere that have made the Elden Ring universe unforgettable.

Elden Ring - Arm of Malenia Mini Replica (1/3 Scale)

Celebrate the unmatched elegance and strength of Malenia, Blade of Miquella, with this exquisite 1/3 scale replica of her prosthetic arm from Elden Ring. Meticulously sculpted and finished, the piece highlights every refined detail - from the intricate golden engravings to the articulated armor plating that defines her graceful yet deadly form. The arm's metallic sheen and subtle weathering evoke the beauty and ferocity of the demigoddess warrior. Presented on a simple black display base, it offers an elegant way to showcase this symbol of unwavering resolve.

Elden Ring - Helmet of Malenia Mini Replica (1/3 Scale)

Honor the legacy of Malenia, Blade of Miquella, with this meticulously crafted 1/3 scale replica of her legendary helmet from Elden Ring. Every detail reflects the beauty and ferocity of the demigoddess warrior, from the intricate engravings to the elegant winged crest that defines her unmistakable silhouette. The helmet's metallic finish and subtle weathering capture the essence of Malenia, Blade of Miquella's battle-worn armor. Presented on a simple black display stand, it offers an elegant and timeless way to display this symbol of strength and determination.

Elden Ring: Shadow of the Erdtree - Helmet of Messmer Mini Replica (1/3 Scale)

Embrace the dark majesty of Messmer the Impaler with this finely detailed 1/3 scale replica of his distinctive helmet from Elden Ring: Shadow of the Erdtree. Sculpted with precision, the piece captures the menacing elegance of Messmer the Impaler's design - from the elongated horns and ornate patterns to the burnished metallic finish that reflects his fiery power. The helmet's intricate craftsmanship evokes the regal yet fearsome aura of the Impaler himself. Presented on a simple black display stand, it provides a refined presentation worthy of this symbol of divine wrath.

Elden Ring Nightreign - Helmet of Wylder Mini Replica (1/3 Scale)

Enter the shadowed realm of Elden Ring Nightreign with this finely crafted 1/3 scale replica of the Wylder Helmet, an iconic piece of armor worn by the wandering knights of the darkened lands. This high-quality collectible captures every intricate detail of the original design, from the weathered metallic finish to the subtle engravings that mark its storied past. The helmet features a fabric neck veil, adding texture and realism to the piece. Presented on a simple black display stand, it offers an elegant way to showcase its imposing form.

Expand Your Collection

Each of these officially licensed mini replicas has been crafted by Pure Arts to faithfully capture the spirit, craftsmanship, and legendary designs of the Elden Ring universe. Whether your allegiance lies with Malenia, your fascination belongs to Messmer, or you're drawn to the mysteries of Nightreign, these collectibles are the perfect way to bring a piece of the Lands Between to your collection.

Which replica will earn a place on your shelf?

items.title: An Obscure Setting Keeps Ruining Elden Ring: Nightreign For Me
items.summary: I do not want to know about any of this
items.content:
I have over 150 hours in Elden Ring Nightreign , and as I have admitted before on this website, I am not very good at it. Over the course of that 150 hours, I think I’ve spent a lot of time being carried by both my partner and our trios pal, who plays Guardian consistently and is great at making sure my wimpy Recluse/Scholar-ass doesn’t die (or, when dead, gets revived promptly). Together, we have taken 150 hours to very slowly kill almost every regular Night Boss in the game, leaving just the DLC’s Dreglord unslain at this time. It is likely due in no small part to my lack of skill that it has taken this long, though I also somewhat blame our busy lives and the fact that we often take long breaks and forget how to play.

But earlier this week, I have found another culprit to pin this on, and her name is Nat. NAT Type.

What the hell is NAT type? I’m still not 100-percent sure despite it being explained to me repeatedly. From what I can gather, it’s some mysterious, internet-related setting that determines how online games connect to the internet and to other people playing those games on the internet. I had literally never heard of it prior to Monday of this week, and I wish I still didn’t know about it.

The reason NAT type came up is because both my partner and I have been having constant issues with disconnects in Elden Ring Nightreign for several months now, for seemingly no particular reason. Almost every single match, one or both of us would disconnect. First, there would be up to 20 seconds or so where our characters would be stuck running around the world, unable to do damage or affect anything in them. Then, we’d actually get kicked out, and have to go through the grueling process of getting back to the menu screen, clicking through some menus, and then reloading back into the game. And because it’s Nightreign , this would be a huge disadvantage. We’d end up wasting something like a full minute of time, and when we got back in we’d either respawn somewhere vaguely near where we disconnected, with all our runes (including one whole lost level) dumped somewhere else for us to go waste time picking up. Or, if we were at the end of a night, we’d just respawn dead, and whoever was still connected would have to maneuver over to us while still fighting the boss and try to get us back up.

This has been infuriating! I tolerated it for a long time, because I enjoy Nightreign , but it really, really feels bad to be the one dragging the group down in this manner.

We tried everything to fix it. Whatever solution you’re about to suggest, we did it. We checked our connections. We reset the router so many times. We changed who hosted the match. We screwed around with all sorts of settings. We made sure we were on wired connections. Etc etc etc. None of it worked.

Finally, my partner did some dedicated research and discovered that something called our NAT type was the problem. Apparently, our NAT types were set to Moderate, which can cause issues with online multiplayer. From what I can figure out, you can change your NAT type properly by following a bunch of complex steps dealing with your router. Or for us on Xbox, we were able to spam the “Test NAT” function in the settings until eventually it swapped our NAT type to Open. When we played hours later, my partner’s was fixed, but mine was not. We checked the settings again, and mine had reverted back to Moderate. We spammed Test NAT again, got it to Open, and we’ve had uninterrupted matches ever since.

So I guess now before I play Nightreign , I have to check this setting every time? This is ridiculous! Why does stuff work like this? I feel like I shouldn’t have to do deep research into an obscure-for-most-people internet setting just to play an online game as it’s intended to be played. I’m not trying to do anything wacky here, I’m literally just getting into a co-op game with two other people, all of whom have excellent internet connections. Most people should not have to know about NAT type, or UPNP (whatever that is) or IPV6 or any of the other weird acronyms I saw while researching this. Like yes, I could probably work this out with time if I sat down and messed around with it long enough, but I don’t have time to do technological research just to bonk a stupid death goop monster around a giant arena without making my friend solo him for 60 seconds at a time at random.

If you’re having trouble with disconnections in Nightreign or Elden Ring PvP stuff or anything like that, consider melting your brain and learning about NAT type. I don’t recommend it, but it did result in me being able to play Nightreign without (unnecessary) frustration, improving my evenings dramatically. However, as soon as I beat up Dreglord, I intend to forget everything I know (very little) about NAT type again for the rest of my life.

items.title: Elden Ring Tarnished Edition Review – A Masterpiece in Your Hands
items.summary: The Elden Ring Tarnish Edition brings together the beloved ARPG and its excellent DLC as one package for the Nintendo Switch 2.
items.content:
Back when it was released in 2024, I gave Elden Ring a score of 98. Four years later, and considering I have well over 1000 hours of play time on PC and PS5, I still wonder if my score was too low. For me, Elden Ring is the absolute pinnacle of FromSoftware’s design philosophy and the gold standard for open world action games. It’s now hard to put myself in the shoes of someone playing Elden Ring for the first time. Considering that around 30-40% of Switch 2 owners don’t have a gaming PC or other high-end console, there’s a good chance that gamers picking up the Tarnished Edition will be dropping in for the first time. Lucky them.

The Tarnished Edition brings together the base game and Shadow of the Erdtree DLC, itself maybe the best DLC ever released for a game. It also includes a handful of new weapons, two new classes, and skins for Torrent, the player’s mount. These add-ons are also available for $4.99 for PC and console games who already own the game. Accessing the game’s co-op and PvP features means having a subscription to Nintendo Switch Online.

If you’ve already played Elden Ring on PC or another console, you’re probably just wondering how it fares on Nintendo Switch 2. Elden Ring on the go sounds like a dream come true. The good news is that it runs just fine, if you’re willing to accept some limitations. Frame rates are capped at 30fps. Textures and ray tracing are a little simplified and a bit blurry, especially in handheld mode. On the other hand, the beauty of Elden Ring is in its art, character and environmental designs. It doesn’t depend on photorealism. In combat, the 30fps throttle is a little more frustrating, and framerates dip a little in the more intense boss battles. Bottom line, the Switch 2 is powerful enough to run Elden Ring and players will have the full experience.

If you’ve never played a FromSoftware game, be prepared for some narrative confusion. The developer is known for stories that are opaque, dense with lore and full of sadness, darkness, and fading hope. With an assist by George R.R. Martin, Elden Ring’s narrative tells of a shattered world. The demigod children of Queen Marika have torn the realm apart. The player takes on the role of a Tarnished, tasked with slaying the corrupt demigods and claiming the title of Elden Lord.

It should be noted that with any FromSoft game, there are fans who dive deep into the lore. At the other end, there are even more players who simply ignore most of the narrative and focus on exploration and combat. Elden Ring rewards either approach. For anyone who’s confused, there’s an immense amount of material online about the characters and their complex relationships.

When it comes to action and combat, Elden Ring represents a major step forward and brings together mechanics explored in other games from the developer. There are few — if any — action RPGs with boss battles as finely tuned as those in Elden Ring. The number of weapons, armor sets, and ways to use magic is staggering in its variety. Like most RPGs, Elden Ring has starting classes but these are largely ignored by players past the first few hours. That said, the Tarnished Edition adds two extremely viable classes in the form of the Heavy Knight and Idus Knight.

Souls games have a well-earned reputation for difficulty, and FromSoftware has resisted adding difficulty options. That’s because they’re built in. Especially in Elden Ring, if players are struggling there are always areas to visit and lower level enemies to kill. There are other weapons or spells to try. The game’s system for summoning Spirit Ashes allows players to call on extremely competent AI companions to help out. Compared to exacting platformers where there is no margin for error, FromSoft’s games feel, if not forgiving, at least balanced and fair.

Outside of combat, exploration is extremely rewarding thanks to a fast travel system and Torrent, your mount. While Elden Ring’s map isn’t the biggest open world it feels immense due to layers of verticality and subterranean areas to explore. No area feels too empty and between the labyrinthine Legacy Dungeons and open landscapes, there’s always something to discover or fight. The Shadow of the Erdtree DLC added a significant amount of new content to an already massive game.

If you haven’t played Elden Ring, and the Tarnished Edition on the Switch 2 has enticed you, please make the leap. I envy you seeing it all for the first time. If you have the game on other consoles or PC and don’t own something like a Steam deck or ROG Ally, the Elden Ring you love is there and intact, but with the visual downgrade that you probably expect. In the end, more Elden Ring is a very good thing.

***Switch 2 code provided by the publisher for review***

items.title: Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition review for Nintendo Switch 2
items.summary: Tarnished Edition sounds about right to me.
items.content:
The Lands Between beckon again, and Nintendo finally gets a release of one of 2022s best games and this time, it includes the DLC Shadow of the Erdtree. Is it worth venturing into the world created by George R.R. Martin, or is it as disappointing as the final season of Game of Thrones? Elden Ring was a game I picked up on PC originally a little after it came out. I promptly played it for a handful of hours and quit. Partly because I was frustrated at the difficulty spikes, partly because something else neat and shiny came out right after I purchased it (Hogwarts Legacy, Star Wars Jedi: Survivor, etc. take your pick.) This newly released Nintendo Switch 2 version gave me the chance to dive back in and see The Lands Between again.

The opening cinematic is nothing new for Elden Ring players and features the same scenes, script, etc. Tarnished Edition’s character creation has 2 new classes, the Idus Knight and the Heavy Knight. The Idus Knight starts with pretty good dexterity and strength scores and comes equipped with armor and weaponry that doesn’t slow you down. While the Heavy Knight, as the name suggests, is more of a beefy tank with very high strength stats right away with heavy armor and weaponry making dodges a little harder.

After the opening cinematic, and character creation, players are dropped into a small opening area that can’t be explored much. After about five to ten minutes of wandering around, your first enemy appears, and it’s a boss right away. Don’t worry about defeating it, I never came close to doing so. After the intro into how insane the difficulty is going to be later, players are dropped into a cave with two directions, go deeper into the cave, or leave. If you go deeper into the cave, it serves as the games tutorial and rewards you with a little bit of extra runes (the game’s money and experience).

Elden Ring’s combat is designed to be very precise. This requires players to stay on their toes and learn enemy patterns. Some enemies you can just walk right up to and hit, even in the middle of their animation. While you’re fighting in Elden Ring take care not to attract too much attention. Fighting one or two low level enemies is easy, but when you start getting a few more, (or an enemy that doesn’t flinch when you hit them along with a few wimps) it’s very easy to die. And die you will……. A lot.

Death, just like in other souls likes, makes you drop all your runes where you died. There is a compass at the top of the screen that helps guide you back to where you died to get your runes back. Be careful, if you die along the way your original drop disappears and is replaced by where you died…. Again.

“Sites of grace” are save points in the game that if you die, you will return to. Eventually, when you rest at a specific site of grace you meet an NPC named Melina, who offers you an accord. This allows you to spend runes to level up your character. When leveling up, pick a single stat and raise it by a point, each point you put into a stat costs an increasing amount of runes. Putting points into vitality increases your hit points while strength increases damage from melee weapons and increases your carry capacity.

Elden Ring is a game that wants you to explore. Don’t just go straight to a boss. That was my mistake the first time playing through. As you explore you gain runes, enemies drop better equipment. There are enemies called Teardrop Scarabs in the opening area that can drop more rare and valuable items, some will even upgrade your rechargeable healing flask.

The Nintendo Switch 2 version graphically isn’t as powerful as the PS5 or Xbox Series X. Is it worth revisiting Elden Ring again if you own this game on other platforms? In short, not really. After just an hour into this version I could already see that the Switch 2 wasn’t fully up to the task. While the game still looks good, there was plenty of slowdown in the open areas. In a game where survival depends so much on very well-timed attacks, and defense, seeing the game skip a few frames at inopportune times will kill the experience. It’s painfully obvious that the Switch 2 struggles to keep up. When compared to the PC version, even on an older gaming rig, I’d much rather play it on PC.

Don’t misunderstand, Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition is still a great game, warts and all. It is frustratingly hard, especially if you end up accidentally bypassing some opening areas and save points (like I did both times I played the opening area). If the Switch 2 is what you have, or want to play Elden Ring on the go, pick it up on Switch 2. But if you have something more powerful to play it on, I would recommend PC personally, but PS5 or Xbox Series X would work just as well.

Note: Bandai Namco provided us with a Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition Switch 2 code for review purposes.

items.title: Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition for Switch 2 means you can now touch grace AND grass
Game Review: Elden Ring – Tarnished Edition (Switch 2)
items.content:
Elden Ring is objectively one of the greatest games of all time. Few would disagree, even if the difficulty barrier and Fromsoftware storytelling kept them from exploring one of the most intriguing open worlds ever created. I played Elden Ring for 100 hours in 2022 on the PS5 at launch, therefore my time with the Switch 2 version was more about performance than the many breathtaking moments and discoveries in that original playthrough. Still, I did not review Elden Ring in 2022 for a very specific reason – my previous attempts at souls games ended with a level of frustration that did not transfer well to the review process. Elden Ring changed everything, becoming my gateway into the genre and one of the most refreshing open world experiences in some time. I have since reviewed and beaten countless soulslike games, understanding the genre and the ‘die to improve’ mantra. The Switch 2 version – Tarnished Edition – comes packed with all the extras (including the fantastic Shadow of the Erdtree DLC). It is full of more features than the original release, but the question on everyone’s mind is this – how does it perform on Nintendo’s latest console?

Before I answer the core question, it is best to set the scene for newcomers. Elden Ring is an action/adventure game set in the Lands Between. Your goal is to become the Elden Lord by repairing the Elden Ring, yet you are a maiden-less tarnished (a banished warrior). Your ancestors were stripped of the Erdtree’s guiding light, and the game ensures it is known that you are very much at the bottom of the barrel. To say more would include me mentioning names, relationships and age-old battles that are best discovered in-game. The narrative is a challenge to piece together – you’ll meet a random NPC, they’ll ask you to do something or tell you their tale, and then you’ll continue on without any markers or clue to how to help them. 20 hours later, something or someone triggers a memory of this chat and a thread may start to form. The overarching narrative of defeating demigods to become the Elden Lord is fairly clear, but all else is draped in shadow and it takes lengthy YouTube vids to decipher the tale. Still, the mystery is welcomed in a medium that is all too quick to tell us everything. A second playthrough removes many of the strengths as you know what’s around most corners, yet there is depth in builds that prolongs the experience.

When I play souls games, I generally go with the sword and board (shield) approach as magic and other more niche approaches require in-depth knowledge of builds. As you are gaining levels and needing to choose which of many attributes to increase, you really need a plan in how you want your character to play. Are they all out attack up close, are they causing bleed, are they shooting spells from distance? Choosing a build is your best way to master the challenges ahead, otherwise you are peppering the stats with a scattergun that only makes bosses harder. On this occasion, I went with a samurai that also dabbled in sorcery. The samurai class uses katanas, precision, bleed and positioning to succeed. By adding a staff in my second hand, I now had spells as a projectile rather than the bow (you can swap around with countless weapons, which is half the fun). This allowed my playthrough 4 years later to be distinct, engaging with features that I didn’t really bother with in 2022. It shows the depth involved, as the game is already a colossus in its best aspect: the open world.

As we know with open world games, they are only as good as their sense of exploration and discovery. If we know there’s a point of interest around the bend, is the journey as good as the destination? Rarely. Elden Ring is best in class as there are so many naturally found secrets across an ever-expanding world. Every player will tell you about the first time they discovered a certain lift down to another world, or when they stumbled out of one massive area only to see an equally massive area reveal itself upon a hill. Many aspects of the map will never be seen by players, which makes discovering them and exploring them rewarding – even if the loot found isn’t making you any more powerful. Finding a site of grace (save point and opportunity to enhance level) is the way to plot out the map, all the way to extremely difficult boss fights and dungeons. Finding a site of grace after half an hour of collecting and fighting brings a sense of relief almost unmatched in gaming. Enemy variety is strong despite some re-used mini-bosses, biomes are diverse and unique, and there are insane moments of lore despite not presenting in a traditional sense. All of this combines to create an open world experience for the ages.

Now, onto performance. I put equal time into docked and handheld on the Switch 2. While a game requiring precision movement and skill is better operated through a general controller, the handheld version here appeared to have better framerates and textures. Elden Ring was never a graphical masterpiece, instead thriving off brilliant art design and lighting. It is clear that the Switch 2 makes some sacrifices to see availability for such a demanding title, but the game plays and looks very good overall as a port. There is some slowdown during boss fights and the distances can pop in a little at times, but I was left impressed (especially handheld) on how well it ran overall. I found this to be stronger in presentation than Final Fantasy 7: Rebirth (the closest comparison in game world and action pace) which may in part be due to the darker tone. Either way, if you are a fan of the game or have always been intrigued this is a great purchase on the Switch 2.

Elden Ring is a juggernaut that will forever be reference in the greatest game of all time discussions. With a movie on the way, the IP will continue to be in the spotlight – now available for gamers on all systems. While Nintendo is not renowned for darker games, 2026 has provided excellent ports to bridge the gap for gamers keen to dabble in both first party and third party offerings. Never has there been a better time to journey through the Lands Between.

items.title: ELDEN RING - RAGING WOLF 1/6 SCALE STATUE
items.summary: Who is the Raging Wolf? Among the first Tarnished to join the Roundtable Hold was Vargram, a warrior of great skill and ferocity. He acquired the title of the Raging Wolf from the white wolf pelt that flowed from his helm. Vargram sought to
items.content:
Who is the Raging Wolf?

Among the first Tarnished to join the Roundtable Hold was Vargram, a warrior of great skill and ferocity. He acquired the title of the Raging Wolf from the white wolf pelt that flowed from his helm. Vargram sought to become the shadow of one of the Empyreans and built his strength relentlessly as he traveled through fallow Limgrave to the golden city of Leyndell. And yet in spite of all his strength, his armor is now worn by another… An unnamed Tarnished now walks the Lands Between in the skin of the wolf. Does this warrior seek the same fate as Vargram, forever stalking at the side of an Empyrean? Will they uphold the Golden Order or supplant it for some new code? Whatever the destination, woe befall upon any who dare block the path.

The most impressive Elden Ring statue yet

Standing at 33 cm/13 inches, it’s one of the largest character statues ever produced for ELDEN RING. Crafted with the attentive supervision of FromSoftware, this full 1/6 scale figure captures each minute detail with masterful skill. The size allows perfect fidelity to the beautiful and dark fantasy atmosphere of the game, including smears of bloody red across blade of the Bastard Sword and the crest of the Iron Roundshield. From the intricate filigrees of its helm to its whisps of silvered fur blown back by an errant breeze to the humble, dusty cloth wraps protecting the feet of its greaves against the mossy stones of the path to Stormveil Castle, it’s a portrait of the implacable will of the Tarnished. All these expertly rendered touches from sculpturer Shinya Yamaoka make this statue a perfect match to the most iconic set from one of the most iconic games of this generation.

Where can I get a Raging Wolf Set statue?

Pre-orders for the Raging Wolf 1/6 scale statue can be placed on the official Bandai Namco website. At this time, based on the production estimates of Gecco studio, these stunning PVC/ABS figures will ship to your home in Winter of 2026. If you are a true aficionado of the game, there is no better purchase to bring the world of Elden Ring to your home or office. It’s a timeless piece for your own collection or an impressive gift for a friend or loved one. And one small note, if you have not yet found this set in the Lands Between for your Tarnished, we recommend you seek the aid of Recusant Bernahl at the Volcano Manor.

Place your order for the Raging Wolf statue on the official Bandai Namco Store.

*This product is available on the Bandai Namco Store in Europe, Australia, the Middle East, India, and the United States.
